# Why Your Torque Wrench Has Stopped Clicking

When a torque wrench fails to click at its set value, it is usually a mechanical failure rather than a calibration issue. Calibration drift typically manifests as an incorrect reading—where the tool clicks too early or too late—but it rarely causes the mechanism to become completely silent across the entire usable range. If you are setting 30–40 ft/lbs on regular hex bolts and hearing nothing past that point, the internal clutch assembly has likely seized or worn out to a degree where slip is no longer possible.

The core issue lies in how torque wrenches function mechanically. Unlike digital sensors that might fail gracefully with an error code, mechanical ratchet systems rely on precise friction control within a spring-loaded pawl and gear system. When you apply force, the mechanism must allow the handle to rotate freely until the preset threshold is reached. At that exact moment, a secondary internal spring compresses or disengages a locking pin, causing the characteristic "click" and preventing further rotation of the drive head relative to the handle.

If this mechanism has stopped working entirely, the internal tension springs have likely lost their elasticity due to metal fatigue or corrosion, or the pawl teeth are sheared off. This is distinct from a bolt breaking because you overtorqued it; in that scenario, the wrench clicked correctly at 30 ft/lbs (or less), and your applied force exceeded the tool's capacity or the fastener's yield strength. The fact that the wrench remained silent through the entire application suggests the slip mechanism never engaged.

Attempting to recalibrate a broken torque wrench is not a viable engineering solution. Calibration involves adjusting the spring tension or the gear ratio to correct specific measurement errors. It cannot repair a seized clutch, replace worn springs, or restore missing teeth on internal gears. Trying to force calibration by hammering the handle or applying extreme load can further damage the precision components, rendering the tool permanently unsafe for use.

From a safety and liability perspective, relying on a non-clicking wrench is negligent. In industries like automotive repair or industrial maintenance, torque specifications are not arbitrary; they ensure proper clamping force without stripping threads or warping surfaces. A silent wrench gives you zero feedback loop. You might apply 60 ft/lbs thinking the tool clicked at 40, resulting in a fastener that is either loose (risking failure under load) or catastrophically stripped if you pushed harder to "make sure."

The only reliable course of action is replacement. While it may seem wasteful given the cost of the tool, using an unverified wrench introduces variables into your assembly process that are impossible to quantify. If budget is a constraint and immediate repair isn't possible, the safest temporary measure is to use a calibrated digital torque sensor with wireless data logging. These devices provide real-time feedback without relying on the mechanical click, allowing you to verify the exact moment of peak load even if the traditional wrench fails.

However, note that switching to a different tool type does not solve the root cause; it simply mitigates the risk while you acquire a new mechanical wrench. Once a torque wrench has suffered a total mechanical failure like this, it is generally considered end-of-life equipment. Continuing to use it compromises the integrity of every joint assembled afterward.
